project-configuration.summary: Configure a Claude Project with concise instructions (role, tone, format, constraints) and well-chosen knowledge files, share it with the right permissions, and understand how knowledge is used when it grows large.
points: Projects are self-contained workspaces with their own chat history, project instructions and knowledge base. Chats inside a Project automatically use its instructions and knowledge.

Split configuration by purpose: project instructions hold short, always-on guidance (Claude's role, audience, tone, output format, constraints, what to do when information is missing); project knowledge holds the reference documents (guidelines, policies, specifications, templates).
Keep instructions concise and focused on general context, key guidelines and Claude's role. Pasting a 30-page guide or a nine-page handbook into instructions buries the rules that matter.
A rule buried in a knowledge file is reference material, not a standing instruction; constraints that must apply to every answer belong in instructions.
Use descriptive filenames (for example `sow-2026-03.pdf`, `staff-list-2026-27.xlsx`) and group related documents; it helps retrieval and lets people reference a document by name.
Keep unnecessary personal data out of knowledge: upload the documents the work needs, not raw customer or HR exports.

Project knowledge uses the chat context window. On paid plans, when knowledge approaches or exceeds the limit, retrieval (RAG) mode activates automatically, expanding capacity up to about 10x; Claude then searches the knowledge and pulls in the relevant parts rather than loading everything. No setup is needed.
Because retrieval fetches knowledge by relevance, short material that must shape every answer (a glossary, key definitions) is safer in instructions than in a large knowledge base.
Uploaded documents are cached, so reusing the same project knowledge across chats counts less against usage limits than re-pasting content.

On Team and Enterprise plans, Projects can be shared with individuals, in bulk by email list, or organisation-wide (where admins allow it). "Can view" lets members use the Project and chat in it; "Can edit" lets them change instructions, knowledge and members. Give edit rights only to maintainers.
Chats inside a shared or public Project stay private to the person who had them unless they share the chat explicitly.
The help centre notes that Google Drive files can be added as knowledge only in private Projects; for a shared Project, upload the files and agree a refresh routine.
Each Project has its own memory space, separate from non-project chats. Free accounts are limited to five Projects.
Do not create one Project per chapter or per user to work around a configuration problem; fragmentation multiplies maintenance and loses cross-document answers.

knowledge-connectors.summary: Manage uploaded knowledge and connectors (Google Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Slack, custom MCP) so Claude works from current, permitted data, with actions kept under human approval and organisational policy.
points: Connectors let Claude access apps and services, retrieve data and take actions. Google Workspace connectors (Gmail, Calendar, Drive) are available to all users; on Team and Enterprise plans an Owner or Primary Owner must enable a connector for the organisation before members can use it.
Enablement is not access: each person authenticates individually (OAuth) before a connector works for them, and connectors are toggled on per conversation.

Claude inherits each person's permissions from the connected service. If you cannot open a file, channel or record in the source system, Claude cannot reach it through the connector either. A "file not found" for a colleague's document usually means it is not shared with you.

Gmail: Claude can search and read emails and metadata (attachment metadata, not attachment content), and can send, reply to and forward. By default Claude asks for approval before each of these actions; on Team and Enterprise plans owners decide whether members may let actions run without asking.
Google Calendar: view events across shared calendars, create, update and delete events, find availability, manage invitations.

Google Drive: search and retrieve files, share, move and trash files (with approval), save Claude-generated files to Drive. Text content only is extracted; images embedded in documents are not processed.

Google Docs added to a private Project from Drive sync with the source, so Claude uses the latest version. An uploaded PDF or file is a static copy that must be replaced by hand when the original changes.
When a document is superseded, remove the old version rather than adding the new one alongside it; conflicting versions produce inconsistent or outdated answers.
Retrieval (RAG) mode for large project knowledge activates automatically on paid plans; there is nothing to switch on.

Custom connectors (remote MCP servers) connect Claude to services not verified by Anthropic. Only connect to servers from trusted organisations, use OAuth (never paste passwords), enable them only in conversations that need them, and watch the tool actions Claude proposes; malicious servers or tool content can attempt prompt injection. On Team and Enterprise plans only Owners can add them.

Organisational policy still governs connector use: keep the per-action approval where a person must sign off outbound messages, route sensitive content (payment details, regulated data) around Claude instead of relying on the model to detect and refuse it, and never use a shared credential with broader access than members have.
Do not dump a whole mailbox or database into project knowledge; supply the documents the task needs.
On Team and Enterprise plans, chats containing synced content cannot be shared, and connectors are available in private Projects.

system-instructions.summary: Write system-level (project or account) instructions that are short, specific and testable: role, audience, output format, explicit criteria, and what to do when information is missing or a request would breach a constraint.
points: Instructions for Claude (account level) apply to all chats; project instructions apply only to chats within that Project. Use the project level for role- and task-specific guidance.

A good instruction names the role, the audience, the exact output format (for example user stories with Given/When/Then criteria, or a table with fixed columns), the style, and the rule for gaps: ask before assuming.

Replace vague adjectives ("be thorough, professional, accurate") with explicit criteria. Define a brand voice with named tone attributes, do/don't pairs, short example sentences and banned words rather than the label "brand voice".
Emphasis does not add information. "YOU MUST", capitals, repetition and "never make mistakes" do not change behaviour; a specification does.

For classification tasks, list the exact categories with a one-line definition and an example each, and add an explicit "unsure" route to a person. Do not instruct Claude to guess the most likely category when uncertain.

Give every absolute rule a branch for the missing case. "Always cite the SOW section" with no provision for uncovered topics pushes Claude to invent section numbers; "cite when a section supports the claim; otherwise say the SOW does not cover it and give no citation" does not.

Handle sensitive data on the input side as well as the output side: for example, replace any student name pasted into the chat with a placeholder and say so, rather than only forbidding names in outputs.
Keep instructions from growing by accretion. When they reach hundreds of words of overlapping rules, rewrite them as a short, prioritised set rather than appending more.
Reference material (style guides, handbooks, bank details, contracts) does not belong in instructions, and sensitive data the task does not need does not belong anywhere in the configuration.
Instructions should stop at the draft; do not instruct Claude to send, publish or write to external systems automatically when a person must review first.
Test instructions with a small saved set of prompts that cover the normal cases, the edge cases and the out-of-scope cases, and rerun it after every change.
Splitting audiences into separate Projects is a valid design only when the audiences are never needed in the same conversation; otherwise specify a format per audience in one instruction set.

configuration-maintenance.summary: Keep Projects, knowledge and instructions current and trustworthy over time: refresh and remove stale documents, update rules when the business changes, control who edits, log changes, test after every change, and inform the people who use the configuration.
points: Knowledge does not update itself. When a source document changes, replace the file, remove the superseded version, and run a prompt that should show the new content (for example the new tagline).
Do not keep old and new versions side by side, and do not rely on an instruction to "prefer the newer document"; only the authoritative version should be present.

When the business changes (a new vendor category, a new policy), update the instruction that encodes the rule, test it on real examples, and tell the team what changed. Per-user prompt workarounds and "add a document about it" do not change the rule.
Claude cannot be retrained by users and does not learn the new categories from usage; configuration is changed by editing instructions and knowledge.
Name an owner for each shared Project. Review knowledge on a schedule (for example quarterly) and whenever a policy changes; remove documents that are no longer relevant.
Keep a changelog and a copy of the last known good instructions outside the Project. Claude has no history of its own configuration and cannot tell you what changed last week.
Match edit rights to roles: two named maintainers with "Can edit", everyone else on "Can view". Six editors with no process is how a shared Project silently degrades.
Keep a fixed regression set of test prompts with saved outputs from launch. After any change, rerun it and compare; when quality drifts, rerun it first to see which behaviours changed.

Diagnose before changing. Audit knowledge for duplicates, superseded versions and unrelated documents, and check instruction length, before rewriting anything or switching model. Change one thing at a time and retest.
Adding more content (Slack history, every new document) to a degraded Project deepens the likely cause; pruning usually helps more than adding.
Memory is per-user conversational context; it is not a mechanism for tracking policy changes or keeping knowledge files current.
Freezing a working configuration is not maintenance; policies change and a frozen Project starts giving confidently outdated answers.
Inform users: when categories, formats or sources change, tell the people using the Project so they know what to expect and can report regressions.
